title: When does booth rent pay off for hairstylists?
summary: Use a weekly break-even calculation to find out when booth rent leaves you more than salon commission. Then test the numbers against a slow week.
meta_title: When Does Booth Rent Pay Off for Hairstylists?
meta_description: Find your booth rent break-even point, compare it with salon commission, and check whether the numbers still work during a slow week.

content.text: Booth rent starts to pay off when the commission you would give up is greater than the rent and any extra expenses you would take on. Start with a typical week, then run the same comparison for a slow week.

If your other expenses are the same in both setups, divide your weekly booth rent by the share of service revenue the salon keeps. For $300 in weekly rent and a salon cut of 40%, divide $300 by 0.40. Your break-even point is $750 in weekly service revenue.

On a 60/40 split, check which side gets 60%. In this example, you keep 60% and the salon keeps 40%. Below $750, commission leaves you more. Above $750, booth rent leaves you more, assuming equal expenses.

body.text: Compare a typical week and a slow week

items.text: At $1,500 in weekly service revenue, with $150 in other expenses under either setup, you keep an estimated $750 on commission or $1,050 on booth rent.
At $600 in weekly service revenue, with the same $150 in other expenses, you keep an estimated $210 on commission or $150 on booth rent.

body.text: Account for expenses that change when you rent

content.text: Ask what each setup includes. Compare what you personally pay for supplies, payment processing, booking software and any other recurring costs. If booth rental would cost you an extra $100 per week beyond the rent, divide $400 by 0.40 instead. Your weekly break-even moves to $1,000.

Use weekly numbers throughout. If you have monthly rent, multiply it by 12 and divide by 52 for a weekly estimate. Estimate one-time setup costs separately, and check what you would owe during weeks you take off.
